title: How Agent Orange Worked
summary: Josh and Chuck explain Agent Orange, the U.S. military herbicide sprayed over Vietnam (and parts of Cambodia and Korea-related spraying mentioned) during the war. They cover its origin with botanist Arthur W. Galston, its use as a defoliant to clear jungle cover, the dioxin (TCDD) contamination and its health effects including birth defects and cancer, Victor Yushchenko's dioxin poisoning, the sovereign immunity barrier to lawsuits and the chemical company settlement, cleanup efforts such as the tree barrier, and Admiral Elmo Zumwalt Jr.'s role and his son's fate. The episode closes with listener mail, a Navy postal clerk's note and a tongue twister.
topics: Department of Veterans Affairs Agent Orange

segments.title: Opening banter and Agent Orange skateboards
segments.summary: Hosts stumble through the opening, joke about the Agent Orange skateboard company and confusion with napalm, and set up the topic of Agent Orange as a very potent herbicide.

segments.title: Herbicide use statistics and Agent Orange as a growth regulator
segments.summary: The hosts cite the scale of herbicide spraying in Vietnam, roughly 11 million gallons of Agent Orange and about 6,000 aerial spraying missions, and note that the chemical was a growth regulator that killed plants by stimulating growth until they dried out. Botanist Arthur W. Galston created it and later campaigned against its military use, quoting his statement that scientific discoveries are morally neutral.

segments.title: Why the jungle was sprayed and environmental damage
segments.summary: The military sprayed to remove jungle cover that hid snipers and enemy movement, and to disrupt the Ho Chi Minh trail in Cambodia. The herbicide destroyed crops, roots and topsoil, and polluted water, creating a cycle of contamination.

segments.title: Dioxin and its health effects
segments.summary: The hosts identify dioxin as the dangerous active ingredient. They explain that dioxins are fat soluble, can bind to hormone receptors and enter cell nuclei, potentially altering DNA and causing birth defects, miscarriages and cancer. Emails with images of affected Vietnamese children are mentioned. The VA's earlier claim of only trace dioxin is disputed, since blood levels in Vietnamese people were far above normal.

segments.title: Agent Purple, cancer link and lawsuits against chemical companies
segments.summary: Agent Purple and Agent Pink are mentioned, named for container stripe colors, with Agent Purple having more dioxin. The hosts discuss dioxin's paradoxical effect on cancer, the WHO classification as a known carcinogen, and how the U.S. government avoided suits through sovereign immunity. Lawsuits instead targeted companies Dow, Monsanto, Hercules and Diamond Shamrock, which claimed they were government contractors; a settlement was paid out.

segments.title: Cleanup in Vietnam and the Ben Tre example
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the scale of the problem, citing Ben Tre where the Red Cross estimated 58,000 of 140,000 residents suffered effects, and about a million people nationwide. They discuss cleanup, including a planted wall of trees that may hold soil or filter contamination, and dioxin's half life of about seven years though it can persist in topsoil.

segments.title: Victor Yushchenko's dioxin poisoning
segments.summary: Ukrainian politician Victor Yushchenko was poisoned with dioxin during the 2004 presidential election. He believes it was deliberate, though no charges have been filed and no one has claimed responsibility. His face was badly scarred, and he survived.

segments.title: Veterans programs and Admiral Zumwalt
segments.summary: The VA set up a program with health exams for veterans and covers children of soldiers, and Korean-related spraying is mentioned. Admiral Elmo Zumwalt Jr. ordered Agent Orange sprayed in the Mekong Delta to counter snipers, unknowingly including where his son was serving. His son Elmo Zumwalt III died of cancer, and Elmo IV has a learning disability. Zumwalt later advocated for victims' compensation.

segments.title: Listener mail and tongue twister
segments.summary: A Navy postal clerk stationed in Rome writes in about mail work and a colleague who is a trivia expert. Another listener, Ryan, sends an 'Irish wristwatch' tongue twister, which the hosts attempt.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts direct listeners to the email address and the HowStuffWorks site for more topics, and the episode ends.
